title: Backglow Lets You Personalize the New MacBook Pro’s Glowing Apple Logo – MacRumors
body:
Apple’s iconic illuminated logo, revived on the latest 14‑inch and 16‑inch MacBook Pro models, now has a third‑party makeover. Designer Juan Buis has released “Backglow,” a free macOS utility that lets users change the colour, intensity and animation of the glowing Apple emblem on the laptop’s lid. By tapping into the hardware‑level control Apple built into the new models, the app offers a level of personalisation that was previously limited to the default white‑on‑black glow, turning a static brand badge into a dynamic, user‑driven light show.

Backglow works by communicating with the MacBook Pro’s built‑in back‑light controller, which was originally intended solely for the Apple logo’s illumination. The free version of the software provides a manual colour picker, brightness slider and a selection of preset hues, while a paid “Pro” tier unlocks advanced features such as animated gradients, synchronized lighting with system events, and the ability to schedule glow patterns based on time of day. Users can also import custom colour palettes or sync the glow with external devices via Bluetooth, opening the door to coordinated lighting across a workspace. Early adopters have praised the app’s low CPU footprint and seamless integration with macOS Ventura and later, noting that the changes persist across reboots and do not interfere with the laptop’s thermal management.

The emergence of Backglow reflects a broader trend of third‑party developers extending the aesthetic capabilities of Apple hardware. Since the reintroduction of the glowing logo in 2021, the feature has been largely decorative, serving as a subtle nod to the brand’s heritage. However, the ability to customize it taps into a growing consumer appetite for personalization—particularly among creative professionals and tech enthusiasts who view their devices as extensions of personal style. Similar custom‑lighting solutions have gained traction on Windows laptops and gaming rigs, but Apple’s tightly controlled ecosystem has historically limited such modifications. Backglow’s success may encourage other developers to explore the niche, potentially prompting Apple to consider more native customisation options in future hardware revisions.

Industry analysts see the app as a low‑risk, high‑reward experiment. Because it operates within Apple’s existing API framework, it does not violate warranty terms or require jailbreaks, mitigating legal and security concerns that have plagued other modding efforts. Moreover, the app’s modest pricing model—offering a free tier with optional upgrades—aligns with the “freemium” strategy that has proven effective in the macOS utility market. While the revenue potential is modest compared to large‑scale software suites, the visibility generated by a novel feature on a flagship product could translate into broader brand recognition for Buis and his development team.

Critics, however, caution that the novelty may wear off for the average user. The glowing logo, while visually striking, is a peripheral element that does not impact performance or productivity. Some reviewers argue that the app’s appeal is limited to a niche audience that values aesthetic flair over functional enhancements. Additionally, there is a risk that excessive brightness or rapid colour changes could become a distraction in shared work environments, prompting corporate IT departments to restrict its use on company‑issued devices.

Looking ahead, Backglow could set a precedent for more interactive hardware features on Apple’s laptops. If user demand grows, Apple might integrate deeper software controls for the logo’s illumination, perhaps tying it to notifications, calendar events, or even health metrics. For now, Juan Buis’s creation offers a playful way to personalize a symbol that has long represented the company’s design ethos, turning the MacBook Pro’s lid into a canvas for individual expression. As the line between hardware and software continues to blur, tools like Backglow illustrate how even the smallest details can become avenues for creativity and differentiation in a saturated tech market.
